text:
Implemented the backend AI subsystem for a team health-alert application using Django REST Framework. Integrated Gemini services with the shared alert data model and exposed backend functionality through the application's REST API.

Built date- and location-based retrieval for relevant health alerts and cached disease context so repeated requests did not require the same supporting data to be rebuilt. Added validation and persistent caches for disease metadata and country-risk results, including refresh handling for new, expired, and failed entries.

Diagnosed a bug in geographic prefix matching that caused incorrect location-based retrieval. Traced the problem through the backend retrieval logic, corrected the matching behaviour, and verified that the relevant alert data was returned for the intended locations.

The project provided practical experience with REST APIs, Django backend development, validation, caching, external AI-service integration, structured data retrieval, and debugging application behaviour across multiple backend components.

Conducted Honours thesis work on generalizable detection of AI-generated face images. Configured five released synthetic-image detector checkpoints and two generator pipelines, then benchmarked four detectors on face images produced by GAN- and diffusion-based generators.

Evaluated both same-generator and cross-generator performance using AUC and average precision. Ran 250 real and 250 synthetic images per generator configuration so detector behaviour could be compared consistently across experimental conditions.

Tested robustness under JPEG compression, cropping, resizing, and StyleGAN3 truncation. These experiments examined whether detector performance remained stable when image characteristics or generation conditions differed from those seen in the baseline evaluation.

Documented the benchmark design, experimental results, and implementation limitations in the Thesis A report. The work developed practical experience with PyTorch-based evaluation pipelines, model benchmarking, robustness analysis, distribution changes, reproducible experiments, and interpretation of machine-learning metrics.

Developed a Python discrete-event simulator for a service system with two server groups, FIFO queues, job redirection, trace inputs, and seeded stochastic workloads. The simulator tracked queue and server state as events changed the system over simulated time.

Tested 11 different allocations of a fixed 12-server system through repeated simulation runs. Compared the configurations under the modelled workload and found that a 6/6 split performed best among the tested allocations.

Used common random numbers and paired 95% confidence intervals to compare competing configurations while controlling experimental noise. Fixed random seeds and validated stochastic samples against target service-time and inter-arrival-time distributions so experiments could be reproduced and checked.

The project provided practical experience with queueing behaviour, stochastic systems, discrete-event simulation, experimental design, statistical comparison, reproducibility, and debugging stateful software whose behaviour emerges over long event sequences.
